prompt: According to the lesson, what takes most of the time in patching?

choices.text: Downloading the update over a slow line
choices.why: Downloading is part of the minute that is easy.

choices.text: Everything around the install
choices.why: Right: when, testing, order, and the machines that cannot take it yet.

choices.text: Typing the apt command on every machine by hand
choices.why: That is automated easily; deciding is not.

choices.text: Waiting for the vendor's advisory to be translated
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson depends on a translation.

prompt: The portal's window is Tuesday night. A flaw on the exploited list is found on Wednesday. What does the lesson's process do?

choices.text: Waits six days for the window, because the window is the agreement
choices.why: A P1 has seven days for everything; the window yields.

choices.text: Patches every machine at once, skipping the rings
choices.why: The rings shrink to hours; they do not disappear.

choices.text: Bypasses the window, by the rule written for P1
choices.why: Right: the bypass is decided in advance, not on the day.

choices.text: Asks each client for permission to interrupt the portal
choices.why: The rule is written in advance precisely so nobody asks on the day.

prompt: Why is a package the firm builds itself a fair stand-in for patching nginx from Ubuntu?

choices.text: Because jatoba-health contains nginx's code
choices.why: It contains a few lines of shell.

choices.text: apt treats both the same way
choices.why: Right: versions, repositories, holds and rollbacks work identically.

choices.text: Because Ubuntu forbids patching nginx in a lab
choices.why: No such rule; the lab simply has no internet.

choices.text: Because a small package can never break anything
choices.why: Size has nothing to do with it.

prompt: What does apt read from a repository before it can install anything from it?

choices.text: The directory listing the web server prints
choices.why: apt does not browse directories.

choices.text: Each .deb file, to find out its version
choices.why: That would mean downloading everything first.

choices.text: The Packages index and the Release file
choices.why: Right, which apt-ftparchive wrote.

choices.text: A signed list of the machines allowed to use it
choices.why: Repositories do not list their clients.

prompt: What does `[trusted=yes]` in the lab's sources line give away?

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the repository uses HTTP on a private network
choices.why: A private network is no signature; anybody who can answer for admin:8000 wins.

choices.text: The ability to roll back, since unsigned packages cannot be downgraded
choices.why: The rollback in the lesson worked with it.

choices.text: The signature check: whoever answers for the server installs anything as root
choices.why: Right. A real repository is signed and named with signed-by=.

choices.text: Encryption of the downloads
choices.why: HTTP was never encrypted; the signature is what proves origin.

prompt: `apt-cache policy` shows 1.1 and 1.0, both with priority 500. Why is 1.1 the candidate?

choices.text: Equal priority, so the higher version wins
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Because it was built second
choices.why: Build order plays no part.

choices.text: Because 1.0 is marked as broken in the Release file
choices.why: Nothing in Release marks a version as broken.

choices.text: Because the newest file on disk is always the candidate
choices.why: apt reads versions from the index, not dates from disk.

prompt: Which machines belong in ring one?

choices.text: The ones the firm cannot afford to lose, so they get the fix first
choices.why: They go last, so a bad update reaches them after it has been caught.

choices.text: A random sample of every department
choices.why: Randomness does not make failure cheap or quickly noticed.

choices.text: Ones whose failure is cheap and noticed fast
choices.why: Right: the IT team's own, a test copy, a vocal user.

choices.text: Machines that have not been patched for the longest
choices.why: Age of patch is not the criterion.

prompt: Why does the lesson read `dpkg-query -W` from each machine after ring two?

choices.text: To trigger the upgrade on machines that missed it
choices.why: dpkg-query only reads.

choices.text: The installed version is the evidence, not the command sent
choices.why: Right, the same habit as lesson 16's verify.

choices.text: To check that the repository still answers
choices.why: dpkg-query never contacts the repository.

choices.text: Because apt does not print what it installed
choices.why: It does; the point is what the machine has now.

prompt: With a P1 flaw and seven days, why does the lesson keep ring one at all?

choices.text: Because the policy forbids skipping a ring under any circumstances
choices.why: No such rule appears; the argument is practical.

choices.text: To give the vendor time to publish a second fix
choices.why: The ring is about catching your own breakage.

choices.text: Because ring one machines are the ones being exploited
choices.why: Nothing says so.

choices.text: An hour on a few machines catches the updates that fail to install at all
choices.why: Right, which is most of the bad ones.

prompt: Before the lesson added 51jatoba, why would unattended-upgrades never install jatoba-health?

choices.text: Because jatoba-health has no security flag in its control file
choices.why: There is no such flag; origins decide.

choices.text: Its origin was not on the allowed list
choices.why: Right: Ubuntu's list holds only Ubuntu's origins.

choices.text: Because it was installed by hand, and those are excluded
choices.why: How a package was installed does not matter.

choices.text: Because unattended-upgrades only runs on servers, not on desk
choices.why: It runs on every Ubuntu machine with it enabled.

prompt: The dry run ends with `All upgrades installed`. What is installed on web afterwards?

choices.text: 1.1, because the line says the upgrades were installed
choices.why: In a dry run the line describes the simulation.

choices.text: Still 1.0, because a dry run changes nothing on the machine
choices.why: Right: --dry-run changes nothing.

choices.text: Both, side by side
choices.why: A Debian package has one installed version at a time.

choices.text: Neither: the dry run removed 1.0 to test the install
choices.why: A dry run removes nothing.

prompt: Where do automatic updates fit badly, according to the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: an update that restarts a service with users connected
choices.why: Interruptions belong in a window.

choices.text: an update that needs a step a person must take
choices.why: Nobody is there to take it.

choices.text: a routine security fix on a workstation
choices.why: That is exactly where they fit.

choices.text: an update that changes how the program behaves
choices.why: Behaviour changes need a test first.

prompt: Why does the lesson call a hold dangerous as well as useful?

choices.text: Because a hold deletes the newer version from the repository
choices.why: It changes nothing in the repository.

choices.text: Because apt ignores holds during security updates
choices.why: Every apt command that upgrades respects it.

choices.text: It never expires and nothing complains about it
choices.why: Right: six months later nobody remembers why.

choices.text: Because a held package stops running
choices.why: It keeps running, at the old version.

prompt: What cheap check keeps holds honest?

choices.text: apt-mark showhold on each machine, against the exceptions
choices.why: Right: a hold with no exception is a finding.

choices.text: Reinstalling every held package once a month
choices.why: That changes nothing about why it is held.

choices.text: Removing every hold before each maintenance window
choices.why: That would install exactly what was held for a reason.

choices.text: Reading dpkg.log for the word hold
choices.why: apt-mark showhold answers the question directly.

prompt: The command that stops apt from upgrading a package on one machine is `apt-mark ___ jatoba-health`.
Why did the rollback on desk work?

choices.text: Because dpkg keeps a copy of every version it ever installed
choices.why: It does not; it fetched 1.0 again.

choices.text: The firm's repository still had version 1.0 to install
choices.why: Right. A repository with only the latest version cannot roll back.

choices.text: Because the package had no configuration files
choices.why: That made it simpler, not possible.

choices.text: Because desk is in ring one
choices.why: Rings decide order, not whether a downgrade works.

prompt: An update migrated the portal's database to a new format. It breaks something. What does the lesson say about rolling the package back?

choices.text: It can work, as long as --allow-downgrades is given
choices.why: The package goes back; the data does not.

choices.text: It is impossible, because dpkg refuses to downgrade database servers
choices.why: dpkg refuses nothing of the kind.

choices.text: The old version may not read the data; a prior snapshot or rolling forward is the answer
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Roll back first and migrate the data by hand afterwards
choices.why: Undoing a migration by hand is the risk, not the plan.

prompt: In dpkg.log, how does the rollback from 1.1 to 1.0 appear?

choices.text: As a remove of 1.1 and an install of 1.0
choices.why: The log shows one line for the change.

choices.text: As a downgrade line
choices.why: dpkg's log has no such word here.

choices.text: As an upgrade from 1.1 to 1.0
choices.why: Right: the versions are what show the direction.

choices.text: It does not appear, because downgrades are not logged
choices.why: It is the third line in the transcript.

prompt: Put the lesson's rollout in order.
items: build both versions and the index on admin
point desk and web at the firm's repository
upgrade desk and check the portal answers
read the installed version back from both

prompt: Match each command with what it does in the lesson.

pairs.right: keeps one package at its version
shows what an automatic run would do

prompt: Under lesson 16's policy, how many days do both rings have for a flaw on the exploited list?
Every machine has unattended-upgrades on. A laptop was off for a month. How does the firm find out it is behind?

choices.text: unattended-upgrades sends an alert when it has missed a day
choices.why: A machine that is off sends nothing.

choices.text: The repository notices that the laptop did not download anything
choices.why: The repository does not track its clients.

choices.text: The inventory reads installed versions from every machine
choices.why: Right, lesson 18's job.

choices.text: It cannot, until somebody reports a problem
choices.why: It can, if it measures; the lesson names how.
